title: Environmental and material implications of global climate mitigation pathways - Nature Energy
gist: Multimodel study coupling 24 IAM pathways (IMAGE, MESSAGEix, REMIND) with prospective life-cycle assessment for 2020–2100: deep decarbonization brings large air-quality/health and ecosystem cobenefits but does not reduce land, water or mineral pressures; for copper, nickel, cobalt and other electrification metals, climate ambition mainly pulls extraction forward in time rather than raising cumulative volumes, while cumulative demand overshoots current reserves (copper 2–5x, nickel 3–7x) in every pathway. Demand reduction and limited CDR reliance are the levers that moderate pressures.

insights.claim: In climate pathways below 2.0 °C, aggregate human health burdens from global final energy provision fall by a median of 8% by 2100, versus a median increase of 65% in pathways above 2.5 °C.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Quantifies the health dividend of decarbonization; supports policy durability of coal phase-out regardless of climate framing.
insights.quote: Aggregate human health burdens, measured in disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), decrease by a median of 8% by 2100
insights.locator: Environmental impacts beyond GHG emissions

insights.claim: Most of the human health benefit of decarbonization arrives early: by mid-century particulate matter formation is already down a median 48% and photochemical ozone formation 43% in sub-2 °C pathways, driven by coal and combustion phase-out.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Coal phase-out front-loads health benefits; the political case for coal exit is strongest in the near term.
insights.quote: Much of the human health benefit is achieved during the first decarbonization steps
insights.locator: These improvements emerge early in the transition

insights.claim: After mid-century, energy-related health burdens rise again across pathways because upstream human toxicity from expanding energy supply chains and mining grows, so pathways retaining residual combustion lose their earlier gains.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Mining-related toxicity becomes the dominant long-run health issue of the transition; expect tightening mining ESG regulation.
insights.locator: Beyond mid-century, health burdens increase again

insights.claim: Socioeconomic narrative matters as much as climate target: among sub-2 °C pathways, SSP1 scenarios cut total human health impacts by a median 21% versus a 6% increase under SSP2, and cut ecosystem impacts 59% versus 41%.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Efficiency, lower population and lower energy demand (SSP1) deliver materially better outcomes than hitting the same temperature via SSP2.
insights.locator: Nevertheless, differences in environmental outcomes are not determined

themes.theme: Electrification's hidden ecotoxicity and water costs

insights.claim: Total ecosystem quality impacts decline 23–68% by 2100 in sub-2 °C pathways but rise up to 119% under warming above 2.5 °C.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Deep decarbonization is net-positive for ecosystems at the aggregate level.

insights.claim: Freshwater ecotoxicity rises in every mitigation pathway analysed, including the most sustainability-oriented SSP1 scenarios where it increases 33–111% by 2100.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Even 'green' pathways worsen metal-driven water toxicity; a regulatory and permitting risk for mining and metal processing.
insights.quote: Freshwater ecotoxicity increases across all pathways analysed
insights.locator: However, this aggregate improvement masks an exception

insights.claim: Electrified transport is the dominant driver of rising freshwater ecotoxicity, contributing an average 70 percentage points (range 37–130) in sub-2 °C pathways, via upstream battery production, electric motor manufacturing and copper-intensive grid and charging infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: EV supply-chain environmental scrutiny will focus on metal mining/refining emissions, not tailpipes; favors cleaner refiners and recyclers.
insights.quote: These impacts arise not at the point of energy use but along upstream supply chains

insights.claim: Reductions in ecotoxicity from coal mining (up to −20 percentage points) and oil refining (up to −15 percentage points) are outweighed by metal supply for electrification, though ecotoxicity still stays far lower below 2.0 °C than above 2.5 °C.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Under-decarbonizing is worse still; the answer is managing mining impacts, not slowing electrification.
insights.quote: additional measures to manage mining impacts and metal supply chains might be needed to limit freshwater ecotoxicity
insights.locator: Even as fossil fuel phase-out reduces ecotoxicity

insights.claim: Electrification of transport, buildings and industry accounts for a median 64% of positive contributions to freshwater use increases in sub-2 °C pathways, mainly from water in mining, material processing and cooling; hydrogen contributes a median 7% and BECCS 2.5%.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Water availability is a material siting constraint for mines and processing plants; water-tech and water-rights exposure rises with electrification.
insights.locator: Freshwater use also increases across nearly all pathways

insights.claim: Freshwater use increases show no consistent relationship with climate ambition within SSP2, meaning they are set by energy-system configuration rather than mitigation level.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Water pressure is a design choice of the transition (technology mix), not an unavoidable cost of ambition.
insights.locator: These increases show no consistent relationship

insights.claim: Net land occupation by 2100 ranges from −13% to +354% across sub-2 °C pathways, a 367-percentage-point spread driven almost entirely by the scale of biomass deployment (transport biofuels, biomass industrial fuels and BECCS).
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Bioenergy-heavy pathways create major land competition; a key risk for biofuel/BECCS-reliant decarbonization plans and for agricultural land prices.
insights.quote: a spread of 367 percentage points driven almost entirely by the scale of biomass deployment

insights.claim: SSP2-based sub-2 °C pathways show the largest land-use increases (median +194%) versus SSP1 (median +67%), while land used for solar PV and wind contributes far less to cross-pathway variation.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Land-use objections to solar and wind are minor relative to biomass; bioenergy scale is the land variable to watch.

insights.claim: Greater climate ambition mainly accelerates the near-term timing of metal extraction rather than increasing total volumes required over the century.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: For metals investors the ambition debate is about the slope of the 2030s demand curve, i.e. price spikes and capex timing, not total resource need.
insights.quote: Greater climate ambition primarily accelerates the near-term timing of extraction rather than raising the total volume required over the century
insights.locator: Timing and scale of metal extraction demand

insights.claim: Under sub-2 °C pathways, copper demand embedded in global final energy provision alone exceeds 2023 global copper production (22.6 Mt/yr) by 2035–2040 in all models, reaching a median 43 Mt/yr by mid-century.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Energy-transition copper demand alone roughly doubles today's total mine output by 2050; bullish long-dated copper supply tightness.

insights.claim: Across pathways, the largest 2040 demand differences arise for lithium (+62%), cobalt (+53%), zinc (+46%) and silver (+43%), with copper and nickel rising more moderately (+24% to +30%).
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Lithium and cobalt have the highest sensitivity to climate-policy ambition; most exposed to policy-driven demand swings.

insights.claim: Cumulative 2020–2100 copper extraction is 3.3–5.0 Gt in sub-2 °C pathways versus 2.3–5.0 Gt above 2.5 °C, and nickel and cobalt ranges overlap across about two-thirds of their extent, because faster electrification is offset by lower long-run energy demand.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Long-run resource adequacy is roughly policy-independent; the investable variable is near-term demand pull-forward.
insights.locator: Despite these pronounced differences in annual demand

insights.claim: Cumulative extraction embedded in final energy provision over 2020–2100 reaches 2–5x current reserves for copper, 3–7x for nickel, roughly 1–7x for cobalt, 1.7–4.4x for silver and 1.4–3.5x for zinc, in every pathway including the least ambitious.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Reserve overshoot under all scenarios implies structural need for exploration, reserve replacement and recycling in copper and nickel regardless of climate policy.
insights.quote: the pressure on primary supply is set by the overall scale of electrification rather than by stringency of the climate target
insights.locator: Accordingly, longer-term availability concerns

insights.claim: Some headline 'critical' metals are not strongly depletion-constrained by energy demand: lithium cumulative demand spans 0.4–4x current reserves, rare earth elements stay at only 1–3% of reserves, and manganese stays modest; their challenges are deployment pace and geographic concentration of mining and refining.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: For lithium and REEs the risk is concentration and refining bottlenecks (geopolitics), not geological scarcity; position for processing capacity rather than reserve scarcity.

insights.claim: Platinum group metal demand falls in the near term as internal combustion vehicles and their exhaust treatment are phased out, then rises later in the century in hydrogen-heavy pathways due to PEM electrolysers and fuel cells.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: PGMs face a near-term demand trough before a hydrogen-contingent recovery; a long-dated optionality bet on hydrogen adoption.
insights.locator: Platinum group metals illustrate a different mechanism

insights.claim: Even with highly optimistic recycling assumptions, the near-term acceleration of metal demand in ambitious pathways stays pronounced and cumulative extraction is only partially moderated.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Recycling cannot close the 2030s–2040s primary supply gap; primary mining capacity remains essential.
insights.locator: The IAM pathways capture endogenous responses

insights.claim: Accelerated near-term metal demand under ambitious climate pathways potentially increases exposure to supply constraints, price volatility and geopolitical pressures in critical mineral supply chains.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Expect more volatile metal prices and more state intervention (stockpiles, export controls) in an ambitious transition.

insights.claim: Lower final energy demand consistently moderates most environmental and material pressures, a relationship the authors say remains underweighted in mitigation strategies that emphasize supply-side substitution.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Efficiency and demand-reduction plays are undervalued relative to supply-side substitution in policy and capital allocation.

insights.claim: Removal-intensive pathways allow higher residual emissions and larger energy systems, so among pathways with comparable climate outcomes they generally carry higher burdens across multiple environmental dimensions, worsening as CDR substitutes for deeper emission cuts.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Heavy reliance on CDR (e.g. BECCS) to meet targets carries hidden environmental costs; a reputational and regulatory risk for CDR-dependent net-zero plans.

insights.claim: The most ambitious REMIND and MESSAGEix pathways exceed 80% wind and solar generation by mid-century, while IMAGE retains larger shares of hydro, nuclear, gas and biomass, which helps explain cross-model differences in non-climate impacts.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Model choice embeds a power-mix bet; investors using IAM scenarios should know which model underlies a forecast.

insights.claim: The authors recommend diversified portfolios of mitigation and CDR technologies to avoid concentrating pressure on specific resources, and energy service demand reduction as an essential complement to technological decarbonization.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Supports policy tailwinds for demand-side measures and technology diversification over single-technology bets.

insights.claim: The study's IAM pathways do not model feedbacks from constrained mineral supply, prices or material availability, and other work suggests such constraints could substantially reshape technology deployment and expose bottlenecks absent from standard IAM projections.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Standard IAM-based metal demand forecasts may understate bottleneck risk; real-world prices will feed back into technology choices.
